title: Look for floor and confidence gains, not just dramatic ceiling jumps
summary: After the beginner phase, aim training often improves the player's bad-run quality and confidence floor slowly enough that it is hard to feel without deliberate comparison.
why: The first gains can feel dramatic, but later gains often show up as fewer terrible reps and more stable baseline execution.
Without tracking floor and consistency, the player may mistake subtle progress for no progress.
actions: Track worst-run quality, consistency, and confidence, not only PBs or highlight runs.
When progress feels invisible, compare a block of sessions instead of trusting one day of feel.
If the floor rose but the ceiling feels flat, keep adjusting the routine rather than concluding the trainer stopped working.
avoid: Do not quit only because improvement no longer feels dramatic from day to day.

drills.label: Consistency review block
drills.query: performance floor consistency review aim training
drills.reason: A consistency-focused review makes subtle progress visible enough to guide the next block.

evidence.claim: Aim trainers often work by slowly raising the performance floor and confidence window in ways that are not immediately obvious.
evidence.excerpt: Aim training very slowly over time raises the floor and the ceiling.
